questions.question: Clustering is a process that groups similar data objects together such that they are dissimilar to objects in other groups.
questions.reasoning: A cluster is a collection of objects similar within the group and dissimilar to objects in other groups.

questions.question: High intra-class similarity means clusters are cohesive, while low inter-class similarity means they are distinctive.
questions.reasoning: Good clustering requires maximizing intra-class similarity (cohesive) and minimizing inter-class similarity (distinctive).

questions.question: Clustering is generally only useful as a stand-alone tool for data distribution insight, not as a preprocessing step.
questions.reasoning: Clustering is useful both as a stand-alone tool and as a preprocessing step for other algorithms like regression or classification.

questions.question: In the context of data mining, compression can be achieved by using cluster centroids instead of all the original data points.
questions.reasoning: Using cluster centroids instead of all data is an example of compression.

questions.question: The partitioning approach to clustering constructs a hierarchical decomposition of the data based on some criterion.
questions.reasoning: The partitioning approach constructs various partitions evaluated by a criterion (e.g., k-means). Hierarchical approaches create a hierarchical decomposition.

questions.question: The K-means algorithm minimizes the Sum of Squared Errors (SSE), defined as the sum of squared Euclidean distances between each point and its assigned centroid.
questions.reasoning: K-means minimizes the sum of squared distances, E=∑∑ p∈Cᵢ (p−cᵢ) 2 , where cᵢis the centroid.

questions.question: The optimal solution for partitioning n objects into k clusters can be found efficiently using Lloyd's algorithm in polynomial time with respect to n.
questions.reasoning: Finding the optimal solution is NP-Hard; K-means is a heuristic method.

questions.question: The complexity of the K-means (Lloyd's algorithm) is O(tkn), where t is the number of iterations, k is the number of clusters, and n is the number of objects.
questions.reasoning: The efficiency is O(tkn), and normally k,t≪n.

questions.question: K-means is guaranteed to terminate at the global optimum of the SSE function.
questions.reasoning: K-means often terminates at a local optimum.

questions.question: If K-means is poorly initialized, it may result in empty clusters (centroids with no points assigned).
questions.reasoning: Empty clusters can occur due to a bad choice of K or a poor initialization.

questions.question: K-means++ is an initialization method designed to choose initial centroids that are close to each other.
questions.reasoning: K-means++ chooses the second centroid with probability proportional to D(xⱼ,c₁) 2 , which gives a point far enough from c₁.

questions.question: K-means is highly robust to noisy data and outliers because it uses the mean to calculate centroids.
questions.reasoning: K-means is sensitive to noisy data and outliers because the mean can be substantially distorted by extreme values.

questions.question: In K-medoids, the cluster center is represented by an artificial point that minimizes the squared Euclidean distance to all points in the cluster.
questions.reasoning: K-medoids uses a medoid, which is an actual data object in the cluster, whose average dissimilarity to all objects is minimal.

questions.question: The PAM (Partitioning Around Medoids) algorithm scales well for very large datasets due to its iterative optimization.
questions.reasoning: PAM does not scale well for large datasets because it checks all substitutions of medoids with non-medoids at every iteration.

questions.question: Hierarchical clustering requires the user to specify the number of clusters ⁽ᵏ⁾ in advance.
questions.reasoning: Hierarchical clustering does not require k as an input, but it requires a termination condition.

questions.question: Agglomerative hierarchical clustering follows a top-down (divisive) approach.
questions.reasoning: Agglomerative clustering (AGNES) is a bottom-up approach.

questions.question: In hierarchical clustering, a dendrogram represents the nested partitioning of data objects.
questions.reasoning: Hierarchical clustering results in a dendrogram, which is a tree of clusters.

questions.question: Cutting the dendrogram at the desired level results in a set of partitions, where each connected component forms a cluster.
questions.reasoning: A clustering is obtained by cutting the dendrogram at the desired level.

questions.question: Single linkage computes the distance between two clusters based on the largest distance between any element in one cluster and any element in the other.
questions.reasoning: Single link uses the smallest distance between elements. The largest distance is used by Complete link.

questions.question: Single linkage clustering tends to find clusters based on local proximities, whereas complete linkage relies on global proximities.
questions.reasoning: Single linkage finds local proximities; Complete linkage finds global proximities.

questions.question: AGNES (Agglomerative Nesting) starts with all objects in one cluster and recursively splits them.
questions.reasoning: AGNES starts with all points in different clusters and merges nodes (bottom-up).

questions.question: DIANA (Divisive Analysis) starts with all objects belonging to the same cluster and recursively splits them until a termination condition is met.
questions.reasoning: DIANA starts with all objects in the same cluster and splits them (top-down).

questions.question: Solving DIANA optimally involves considering²n −1 ways of partitioning n objects, which is computationally inexpensive.
questions.reasoning: Considering²n −1 ways is very expensive; DIANA uses greedy heuristics to reduce complexity.

questions.question: The single-linkage hierarchical clustering problem is mathematically equivalent to finding the Minimum Spanning Tree (MST) in a connected, weighted, and undirected graph.
questions.reasoning: Single-linkage and MST problems are equivalent.

questions.question: The K-means algorithm uses "greedy optimization," similar to Kruskal's algorithm for MST.
questions.reasoning: K-means uses "alternating optimization" or "block coordinate descent". Kruskal's is greedy optimization.

questions.question: The use of gradient descent is generally beneficial for solving K-means, allowing it to always converge to the optimal solution.
questions.reasoning: K-means (Lloyd's algorithm) uses alternating optimization, not typical gradient descent, and is not guaranteed to find the optimal solution.

questions.question: If random initialization of centroids for K-means is poor, this may result in empty clusters.
questions.reasoning: Empty clusters can result from a poor initialization.

questions.question: K-means clustering can be viewed as a form of compression of N data points to K centroids, minimizing the approximation error.
questions.reasoning: K-means minimizes approximation error of representing every data point by its nearest centroid.

questions.question: For K-means clustering, the error will always be exactly 0 if we set the number of clusters K equal to log(N), where N is the number of data points.
questions.reasoning: The error is only guaranteed to be 0 if K=N (each point is its own centroid).

questions.question: In practice, to achieve better performance in clustering accuracy for K-means, it is recommended to use the same initialization every time rather than initializing randomly.
questions.reasoning: Random initialization is used to explore different local optima; for better performance, one should not use the same initialization every time (e.g., using K-means++ or multiple random restarts).

questions.question: The DIANA (Divisive Analysis) hierarchical clustering algorithm traces exactly the same clusters as a bottom-up (agglomerative) approach would do.
questions.reasoning: DIANA and AGNES perform hierarchical decomposition, but DIANA is divisive (top-down) and AGNES is agglomerative (bottom-up). They may not trace the same clusters, especially since DIANA uses greedy heuristics.

questions.question: Solving K-means clustering optimally is an NP-Hard problem.
questions.reasoning: The optimal solution for partitioning is NP-Hard.

questions.question: If there are 3 actual clusters in the data and we choose K=10 for K-means, the algorithm will automatically return exactly 3 non-empty clusters.
questions.reasoning: K-means will attempt to find 10 clusters, and may result in more than 3 non-empty clusters or potentially empty clusters.

questions.question: A key challenge in cluster analysis is scalability, requiring algorithms to work only on small samples of data instead of the entire dataset.
questions.reasoning: Scalability requires clustering all the data instead of only samples.

questions.question: K-Medoids minimizes the Manhattan distance, whereas K-Means minimizes the Euclidean distance.
questions.reasoning: The medoid minimizes the Manhattan distance (in 1D/median context, generalized to K-medoids). K-Means minimizes Euclidean distance.

questions.question: The centroid linkage method calculates the distance between two clusters by measuring the distance between their medoids.
questions.reasoning: Centroid linkage uses the distance between the centroids (means). Medoid linkage uses the distance between the medoids.

questions.question: The agglomerative clustering approach (AGNES) uses single-link distance by default, meaning it merges clusters with the least dissimilarity.
questions.reasoning: AGNES uses the single-link approach, merging nodes with the least dissimilarity (minimum distance).

questions.question: In DIANA, complexity is reduced by using a greedy heuristic that picks the object with maximum dissimilarity from the rest and moving it to a new cluster.
questions.reasoning: DIANA uses greedy heuristics, including picking the max dissimilarity object to start a new cluster.

questions.question: An important partitioning criterion in clustering is the similarity measure used, which can be distance-based (e.g., Euclidean) or connectivity-based (e.g., density).
questions.reasoning: Similarity measures can be distance-based or connectivity-based.

questions.question: When performing K-means, the SSE necessarily decreases or stays the same with every iteration.
questions.reasoning: K-means uses an alternating optimization approach where each step (assignment or centroid recalculation) reduces or maintains the SSE until convergence to a local minimum.

questions.question: Because K-means utilizes random initialization, multiple runs are necessary to obtain a good estimate of the SSE and Silhouette score.
questions.reasoning: Because K-means uses randomized initialization, multiple iterations per K value are needed to get a good estimate.

questions.question: The medoid of a cluster is defined as the object whose minimum dissimilarity to all objects in the cluster is minimal.
questions.reasoning: The medoid is the data object whose average dissimilarity to all objects in the cluster is minimal.

questions.question: Outlier detection is a possible application for clustering, where outliers are often viewed as points far away from any cluster.
questions.reasoning: Outlier detection is listed as a clustering application.

questions.question: Soft clustering requires that every data object is exclusively assigned to exactly one cluster.
questions.reasoning: Hard clustering requires exclusive assignment. Soft clustering allows for soft or fuzzy boundaries.

questions.question: The efficiency of K-means is primarily dependent on the number of features (dimensions) rather than the number of data points.

questions.question: If K-means is run on data containing a substantial outlier, the final SSE value is expected to be significantly larger compared to running K-means on the original data without the outlier.
questions.reasoning: K-means is sensitive to outliers, and the outlier will increase the SSE dramatically.

questions.reasoning: Dendrograms represent the results of Hierarchical clustering.

questions.reasoning: In some cases (like MST using Kruskal's), greedy optimization yields a global optimum.

questions.reasoning: K-means (Lloyd's algorithm) uses "alternating optimization" or "block coordinate descent".
